source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA), arXiv 2402.08113 tables 1-4
finding: Re-read the accuracy tables. The text list of average drops (-5.1, -7.7, -17.8, -17.9, -20.1) is in absolute points, but the sentence 'gpt-3.5 average drop 37.4%' is a relative drop. Both describe the same GPT-3.5 row. The mismatch is resolved.
numbers: Table 1 (MedQA, 7 bias prompts). GPT-4: no-bias 0.727; self-diagnosis .698, recency .679, confirmation .725, frequency .627, cultural .681, status quo .679, false consensus .625. GPT-3.5: no-bias 0.497; .288, .333, .407, .274, .277, .361, .239. My mean of the 7 biased cells: GPT-4 0.673 (-5.4 points, -7.4% relative); GPT-3.5 0.311 (-18.6 points, -37.4% relative). False-consensus drop for GPT-4: 0.727 to 0.625 = 10.2 points = 14.0% relative (the paper's 14.0%).
limits: PDF table text is column-shifted, so I matched cells to models by checking against the paper's own quoted numbers (72.7, 49.7, 0.627, 23.9, 14.0, 37.4). Mixtral and the small models were not matched cell by cell. Multiple choice, single letter answer, no reasoning allowed.
agent_relevance: Use relative and absolute drops separately in our own reports. BiasMedQA tests letter-only answers, so it measures fast mode only; a scaffold's challenge step is untested here.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models, npj Digital Medicine (published version)
finding: The published version keeps the same mixed wording. Average drops are listed as -5.1 (GPT-4), -7.7 (Mixtral), -17.8 (GPT-3.5), -17.9 and -20.1 (Llama-2-70B), -9.6 (PMC-LLaMA), then separately 'gpt-3.5 average drop in accuracy of 37.4%'. False consensus is worst (24.9% averaged across models), then frequency (18.2%), recency (12.9%), confirmation least (8.1%).
numbers: GPT-4 worst case false consensus -14.0% (p=3.8e-8); confirmation -0.2% (p=0.91). GPT-3.5 worst case 23.9% accuracy. GPT-4 and Mixtral lowest overall reductions (-5.36%, p=1.3e-4; -7.81%, p=1.6e-7); other models dropped 50% or more from original performance.
limits: The paper never says which drops are absolute and which relative. My recomputation (d01) supports absolute for the list and relative for 37.4%.
agent_relevance: Ranking claim in K15 stands: GPT-4 least affected, false consensus worst. Cite the per-model drops only with a stated definition.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA mitigation strategies (education, one-shot, few-shot), arXiv tables 2-4
finding: Warning text and bias demonstrations restore most of GPT-4's loss but little for weaker models. This is a prompt-level 'challenge' step, not a reasoning step.
numbers: GPT-4 mean over the 7 biased cells: baseline 0.673 (no-bias 0.727, gap 5.4 pts); education 0.709 (no-bias 0.727, gap 1.8); few-shot 0.749 (no-bias 0.757, gap 0.8). Frequency bias with education: 0.627 to 0.720 (paper). GPT-3.5 and Mixtral: 'only marginal improvements' with education (paper text). Few-shot and one-shot had many N/A cells for GPT-3.5 and PaLM-2 (safety filters).
limits: Means are mine. Few-shot also changes the no-bias baseline. One run per cell; no confidence intervals in the tables. No chain-of-thought used.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: a short challenge or demonstration closes about 70 to 85 percent of GPT-4's gap but not the weak models'. Keep 'name the planted claim and test it' as a candidate and test it with reasoning on.

source: Zuo, Wan, Wang (2026) Patient cognitive bias in LLM-supported health consultations: simulation-based comparative study, J Med Internet Res 28:e85770
finding: The 2026 JMIR dual-system result is real. A simulated patient pushes a wrong self-diagnosis over 3 dialogue rounds. A conversational model (System 1) takes the history; o1-mini (System 2) gives the final answer. Prompt mitigations and lower temperature helped little.
numbers: 1,273 MedQA-USMLE cases, 6 foundation models, 3 repeated runs, temperature 1.0, patient agent GPT-4o-mini. Biased accuracy foundation-only vs dual: Gemini 1.5 Pro 65.8 to 75.5; Flash 48.5 to 67.3; Flash-8B 35.5 to 65.8 (+30.3); GPT-4o 73.8 to 72.8 (-1.0); GPT-4o-mini 47.5 to 67.2; GPT-3.5-turbo 25.0 to 63.7 (+38.7). Standard (unbiased) dual gains +2.9 to +17.0. The '10 to 39 points' in the abstract is the biased-condition gain range, and it excludes GPT-4o.
limits: Simulation only; explicit self-diagnosis anchor, a high-intensity bias. Multiple choice. Authors state the dual design 'incurs higher reasoning costs'; no token or cost matching is reported.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 4 on 'is it real': yes. The design is a model swap at the last step, not a mode router.

source: Zuo, Wan, Wang (2026) JMIR e85770, o1-mini standalone reference row
finding: The strongest comparison in the paper is missing from the dual-system claim: o1-mini alone, under the same multiturn protocol, beats every dual configuration. So the gain cannot be credited to the System 1 / System 2 split. It may be only the stronger model. It was not matched on tokens.
numbers: o1-mini standalone: 87.2% (SD 0.8) standard, 85.1% (SD 0.5) biased. Best dual result: 85.2% standard (GPT-4o), 75.5% biased (Gemini 1.5 Pro). Recovery of bias-induced loss 89.5% to 138.6% for five models; -11.8% for GPT-4o.
limits: The authors describe o1-mini as a 'contextual comparison', not a baseline. They did not test o1-mini doing the history taking too, or a dual pipeline at matched tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answer: not token-matched, and dominated by simply using the reasoning model alone. Weak support for K16-style switching. It supports K13/K19 more: a stronger reasoning model resists a planted anchor (-2.1 points).

source: Moell, Aronsson, Akbar (2025) Medical reasoning in LLMs: an in-depth analysis of DeepSeek R1, Front Artif Intell
finding: Length statistic and error list re-read. Wrong answers have longer reasoning, but the test rests on 7 wrong answers and the authors themselves say length may mark uncertainty. No test of whether forcing a short answer helps.
numbers: n=100 MedQA cases, 93 correct. Welch t = -2.74, p = 0.032; mean 8,118 characters (wrong) vs 3,648 (right). Error table of 7 wrong answers: protocol misapplication 2, anchoring 1, etiology-consequence confusion 1, lab overinterpretation 1, isoform confusion 1, overinvestigation 1. In one case the reasoning picked the right option but the output letter was wrong.
limits: Only 1 of 7 errors is labelled anchoring (1% of cases), though the text says anchoring and confirmation appear 'across multiple cases'. Authors suggest rerunning long attempts with an added prompt; they did not test it. Cases are 'selected', not a random draw.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: length is a difficulty and error marker (K04 holds), with no causal test. A length-triggered re-check is cheap to test.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Mitigating cognitive biases in clinical decision-making through multi-agent conversations using LLMs, J Med Internet Res 26:e59439
finding: Open-ended diagnosis with GPT-4 Turbo on 16 published case reports where a bias caused a misdiagnosis. Agents had named roles: a devil's advocate for anchoring and confirmation, and a senior doctor for premature closure. This is a forced challenge and differential step.
numbers: First-responder initial diagnosis 0/80 correct in all frameworks (cases were chosen because the first answer was wrong). After discussion, top-2 differential correct 61/80 (76%) in Framework 4-C; humans 13/48 (27%); OR 3.49, P=.002. 16 scenarios x 5 repeats x 3 frameworks = 240 responses.
limits: The 0% start is by case selection. Scores are top-2 after discussion vs one initial answer, so metrics differ. No single-agent GPT-4 with the same extra tokens. Multi-agent costs more tokens, not counted. Human comparison not matched in knowledge or time.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the only open-ended test found. It supports a forced differential or challenge step but has no equal-token control, so it cannot say whether the roles matter or only the extra calls.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician, arXiv 2412.10849
finding: o1-preview on open-ended NEJM clinicopathologic cases. It always writes a differential. Top-1 is right about half the time and the correct diagnosis is in the list about four times in five. No bias manipulation and no anchoring test.
numbers: NEJM CPC 143 cases: correct diagnosis in differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7 to 84.8); first diagnosis correct 52% (44 to 61). Before vs after training cutoff 79.8 vs 73.5 (p=0.59). On 70 cases used with GPT-4: exact or very close 88.6% vs 72.9% (p=.015). Correct next test chosen 87.5%.
limits: Two-reader agreement 120/143 (84%, kappa 0.66). Not a test of anchoring. Preprint version read.
agent_relevance: Shows a gap between list recall (78%) and top-1 (52%) on open cases: the diagnosis is often available but not chosen, so the ranking step, not recall, is the weak point.

source: McDuff et al. (2025) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models, Nature
finding: Clinicians given an LLM differential tool improved, but the paper says clinicians anchored on their own first differential, and the model could be led by clinicians' follow-up questions.
numbers: Top-10 accuracy: AMIE alone 59.1% vs unassisted clinicians 33.6% (P=0.04); clinicians with AMIE 51.7% vs clinicians with search 36.1% (McNemar 45.7, P<0.01).
limits: Anchoring is a post-hoc explanation from clinician feedback, not measured. Two-stage design may increase it.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on the first list is documented as a limit of AI assistance. For our agent, the first draft differential should not be handed to later steps without a challenge.

source: Japanese randomized trial (2020) Availability bias causes misdiagnoses by physicians: direct evidence from a randomized controlled trial, Intern Med
finding: An independent conceptual replication of the availability-bias induction (Mamede 2010) succeeded in the bias but failed in the repair: reflective reasoning did not fix the errors.
numbers: 46 internal medicine residents randomised to control or experimental group; 8 cases (3 look-alikes of dengue fever, 1 dengue, 4 fillers). Control scored higher on experimental than filler cases (0.80 vs 0.59, p<0.01); experimental group did not (0.66 vs 0.64, p=0.756). 71 to 100% of look-alike misdiagnoses in the bias group were dengue. No difference between non-analytic and reflective scores in any case.
limits: Small N, one disease. Different reflection procedure from Mamede. The control-group result implies the look-alikes were easier than fillers, so the design is not clean.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: Mamede's reflection effect is not replicated independently. Keep K03 contested.

source: Mamede and Schmidt (2023) Deliberate reflection and clinical reasoning: founding ideas and empirical findings, Med Educ
finding: A review by the originating group. The replications it lists come from the same group (Mamede, Schmidt, van Gog and co-workers). Reflection helped on complex cases, not simple ones; for students it hurt on complex cases. Bias-induction studies were followed by reflection that restored accuracy.
numbers: Residents' accuracy improved by more than 35% with deliberate reflection on complex cases (no gain on simple cases); students showed the reverse pattern. Availability primes: Wikipedia page study (Schmidt 2014) and prime-by-checking study (Mamede 2010) both repaired by reflection.
limits: Authors review their own work. Independent tests: d10 (failed repair) and van den Berg 2021 (no bias induced; b05). No LLM test of the reflection procedure was found.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 answer: no independent successful replication in humans, no LLM test. Reflection benefit depends on case difficulty and expertise, which fits a difficulty-gated step.

source: Bago and De Neys (2017) Fast logic?: examining the time course assumption of dual process theory, Cognition 158:90-109
finding: Abstract re-read (PubMed). The full text sat behind a bot check and a paywall, so exact percentages stay unread. Four experiments with a two-response paradigm: people often give the correct logical answer first, fast, with high confidence, under load or deadline.
numbers: No percentages available to me. The abstract says correct first answers were 'frequently' observed across four experiments (deadline, concurrent load).
quote: Fast and automatic Type 1 processing also cues a correct logical response from the start.
limits: Gap 6 stays open on numbers. Tasks are syllogisms and base-rate items, not medicine; the load manipulation may not fully block deliberation.
agent_relevance: Mode choice is not 'fast = wrong'. For LLMs a first answer should be checked by a signal, not assumed wrong.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet, ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: The nearest LLM analogue to the two-response paradigm: a first answer, then a second pass. Without an outside signal the second answer is not better and often worse. The model cannot tell when its first answer is right.
numbers: GPT-3.5, standard vs 2 rounds of intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. With oracle labels telling it when to revise: GSM8K 84.3, CSQA 89.7, HotpotQA 29.0 (GPT-3.5) and 97.5, 85.5, 59.0 (GPT-4). In GSM8K the answer stays the same 74.7% of the time; changes go more often from right to wrong.
limits: General reasoning tasks, not medical; older models. Newer reasoning models trained for self-checking may differ. The second sample is a revision, not an independent sample.
agent_relevance: A second pass without a trigger does not help; the trigger carries the value, which is the De Neys point. Test routing with an external check, not an 'are you sure?' prompt.

source: Nori, Usuyama, Horvitz (2024) From Medprompt to o1: exploration of run-time strategies for medical challenge problems and beyond, arXiv 2411.03590
finding: Closest cost-aware comparison on MedQA. The reasoning model wins at higher cost; few-shot hurts the reasoning model; ensembling still helps. No routing between modes was tested; the paper lists metareasoning as future work.
numbers: MedQA US 4-option (1,273 items): GPT-4 0-shot 78.9%, GPT-4-Turbo 5-shot 81.4%, GPT-4o 0-shot 84.4%, GPT-4 Turbo Medprompt 90.2%, o1-preview 0-shot 96.0%. Cost ladder: 88% to 92% to 96% each needs about 10x the price ($5, $50, $500) with GPT-4o few-shot, GPT-4o Medprompt, o1-preview 5x ensemble. o1-preview cheaper than GPT-4 Turbo Medprompt. Prices per 1M tokens: o1-preview 15 in / 60 reasoning / 60 out; GPT-4o 2.5 / 10.
limits: Cost, not token count, is the matched variable and only on the Pareto plot. 3 runs per config for o1. Benchmark near saturation.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 evidence: equal-cost routing is untested on MedQA. The Pareto data give prices to plan a test. A router sending easy items to GPT-4o and hard ones to o1 would need a confidence signal and has no published result.

source: Nori et al. (2024) From Medprompt to o1, section 4.4 reasoning tokens
finding: Within o1-preview, prompting for longer thinking raised accuracy, which cuts against reading long reasoning as a cause of error.
numbers: Paper states accuracy 'tends to trend upwards when more reasoning tokens are used' across benchmarks (Figure 7); exact values only in the figure.
limits: Prompted length differs from natural length. The effect is between prompts, not within items.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: natural long reasoning marks hard items (Moell), but prompted extra reasoning helps. Length is a symptom; do not cap tokens blindly.

source: Xiong, Jin, Lu, Zhang (2024) Benchmarking retrieval-augmented generation for medicine (MIRAGE/MedRAG), ACL Findings
finding: Retrieval of documents (textbooks, PubMed; 32 snippets) against chain-of-thought alone, zero-shot. For exam diagnosis questions (MedQA-US) retrieval gave no gain or a loss. It helps on literature questions (PubMedQA).
numbers: MedQA-US accuracy CoT vs RAG: GPT-4 83.97 to 82.80; GPT-3.5 65.04 to 66.61; Mixtral 64.10 to 60.02; Llama-2-70B 47.84 to 44.93; PMC-LLaMA 44.38 to 42.58. PubMedQA*: GPT-4 39.60 to 70.60. Averages over 5 sets: GPT-4 73.44 to 79.97; GPT-3.5 60.69 to 71.57.
limits: Retrieves documents, not similar patient cases. Not token-matched (32 snippets add large context). Older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: document retrieval does not beat plain CoT on MedQA; the similar-case version has no test found here. A rare-disease agent paper (Nature 2026, PMC12999473) uses case retrieval but was not read.

source: Griot et al. (2025) Large language models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning, Nature Communications
finding: A routing signal based on stated confidence is weak: most models said confidence 5 on nearly everything. Where confidence varied, it tracked accuracy.
numbers: MetaMedQA, n=1,373, 12 models. Only GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, GPT-4o and Qwen2-72B used varied confidence. High-confidence accuracy 56.9%, 83.2%, 77.9%; medium 44.8%, 45.9%, 59.3%; low 16.7% for GPT-4o (CI +-32.7). Models rarely chose 'none of the above' when no option was right.
limits: Verbalized confidence on multiple choice; no routing experiment. Older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a confidence router needs a better signal than the model's stated number: use agreement across samples or an external check.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: reasoning models can learn when to think, arXiv 2505.13417
finding: A trained fast/slow switch for reasoning models (Thinking vs NoThinking). Not medical. It counts response length, so a token account exists.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on three math sets: average response length down 53% and accuracy up 2.4%. NoThinking reported better than Thinking on simple tasks in both performance and efficiency.
limits: Needs RL training; math only; 1.5B model. Not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a learned switch, not prompt-level. The transferable idea is difficulty-gated thinking; the medical version is untested.
